titre: A Man Hidden Beneath Picasso's *La Chambre bleue* (*The Blue Room*)
accroche: Without the money for a new canvas, Picasso paints over a finished portrait. A century later, no one knows who it shows.
contenu_vulgarise:
*La Chambre bleue* (*The Blue Room*), painted by Pablo Picasso in Paris in 1901, shows a woman bathing in the artist's studio. The painting belongs to the Phillips Collection in Washington. In a 1954 letter, a conservator notes something odd in the brushstrokes visible on the surface: they do not match the painted composition.

It is not until the 1990s that X-ray and infrared examinations hint at another composition beneath the visible layer, without producing a clear image. No one yet knows it is a portrait.

## A Face Beneath the Color

In 2007, the Phillips Collection begins a new study of the painting, with the conservator Patricia Favero. In 2008, an infrared camera fitted with a spectral filter that passes long wavelengths sees through the blue paint with unprecedented clarity: it reveals the face and torso of a bearded man in a jacket and bow tie, his head resting on his hand, three rings on his fingers.

The investigation widens in 2012. Teams from the National Gallery of Art, Cornell University and the Winterthur Museum join the Phillips Collection. The painting is scanned by X-ray fluorescence, a method that detects chemical elements such as mercury, iron or cobalt without taking samples; twelve tiny paint samples are also analyzed at Winterthur to identify the buried pigments. A meeting of the teams in April 2014 draws conclusions: the pigments in the two compositions are identical, which makes it more likely that both are by Picasso's hand, and the portrait, though unsigned, appears to be a finished picture. Examination of paint cross-sections under the microscope finds no trace of fresh paint being picked up: the paint of the portrait was mostly dry when Picasso painted over it, possibly with as little as three or four months in between.

The reason for this recycling is not mysterious. Picasso is working in Paris, and a new canvas is expensive. A curator at the museum, Susan Behrends Frank, sums it up simply: when he had an idea he had to get it down, and he could not afford to buy a new canvas every time; he sometimes even painted on cardboard, which was cheaper than canvas. He therefore hurriedly covered another complete picture.

## A Name Still Missing

One question remains that science has not resolved: who is this man? Researchers have ruled out a self-portrait. One name circulates, that of the Parisian art dealer Ambroise Vollard, who hosts Picasso's first show in 1901; but no document and no clue left on the canvas can confirm it.

What *La Chambre bleue* reveals therefore goes beyond a technical feat. An X-ray does not restore an identity: it makes visible a shape, a face, a posture, not the name of the person who bears them. It took a remark in 1954, examinations in the 1990s and a collaboration among four institutions for the hidden portrait to be made public in June 2014, and the man was still anonymous.

repere.texte: X-ray and infrared examinations carried out in the 1990s hint at a hidden composition, without a clear image. The conservator Patricia Favero begins studying the painting in 2007. A collaboration among four institutions (Phillips Collection, National Gallery of Art, Cornell University, Winterthur Museum) then carries out analyses, including X-ray fluorescence in 2012.

carte.punch: Without the means for a new canvas, Picasso paints La Chambre bleue over a portrait of a man.
carte.idee: Beneath Picasso's La Chambre bleue (The Blue Room, 1901) lies the portrait of a bearded man in a bow tie, hinted at by X-rays in the 1990s and revealed by infrared in 2008. His identity remains unknown in 2014, when the portrait is made public.

quiz.question: How do researchers establish the presence of the hidden portrait beneath La Chambre bleue and its link to the painting?
choix: By comparing Picasso's signature with the one found on other canvases painted in Paris during his Blue Period, between 1901 and 1904
By finding, in the Phillips Collection's archives, a letter in which Picasso himself describes the picture he painted over
By combining infrared imaging, which reveals a face beneath the painted layer, with an analysis of the pigments and paint cross-sections
By questioning the descendants of the Parisian art dealer Ambroise Vollard about a portrait that has since vanished
quiz.explication: Infrared imaging, in 2008, reveals the face and torso of a man beneath the blue layer; in 2012 and after, X-ray fluorescence analysis, samples and examination of paint cross-sections show that the two compositions share the same pigments and are close in time. No compared signature, no letter from Picasso and no descendant questioned play any part in this demonstration.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which imaging reveals the face of the hidden man beneath La Chambre bleue in 2008?
choix: An infrared camera fitted with a spectral filter
Preparatory drawings found in Picasso's studio
A cleaning of the blue paint layer
quiz_supplementaire.explication: An infrared camera fitted with a spectral filter produces a clear image of the face and torso in 2008; the 1990s examinations had only hinted at a hidden composition, without a clear image.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did Picasso paint La Chambre bleue over an already finished portrait?
choix: He judged his first portrait a failure and wanted to start over
The sitter had asked for the portrait to be erased
He lacked the money to buy a new canvas
The original canvas had been damaged by the damp of his studio
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to a curator at the museum, Picasso could not afford to buy a new canvas for each idea, and he sometimes painted on cardboard, which was cheaper.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which name is suggested, without proof, for the man hidden beneath La Chambre bleue?
choix: Guillaume Apollinaire, poet and art critic
Max Jacob, Picasso's friend and roommate
An anonymous client of Picasso's studio
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The name of Ambroise Vollard, who hosts Picasso's first show in 1901, circulates without any document to confirm it.
